e17-emuA:
The basic technique of hearthwork is that if you need counseling, you ask several people to help you one after the other, each giving you the same amount of time that you’ve given them, and giving you their complete attention. No interpretation, no fixing, just pay attention, then switch.

The idea is that the capacity to be there for people when they need help isn’t located in a few “professionals” or gurus or the most emotionally available (aka indispensable) founder of the group, but in the community as a whole.

Another thing is that the person you’re working with shouldn’t have power over whether or not you can be a member of the group, whether or not you can work for the group, whether or not you can live at the group, whether or not you can see your kids, whether or not you can get medication, whether or not you’re right about something you’re arguing about, etc. Giving someone the job of taking care of people emotionally and giving them administrative power is just creating a new hierarchy.

Another thing is knowing what kinds of things to refer to outside or expert assistance for.

One thing is to deal with jealousy and conflict before it gets put on the agenda (generally at the bottom of the agenda).

Also, read my Romance Guide , because no matter how much your founding document says that you’re all beyond romance, you’re still gonna have dyads.
e17-emuB:
Hearthwork relies on peer-distributed counseling: everybody gets the same amount of time to simply listen to each other, without interpreting or fixing, and then switch.

This means that the community’s counseling capacity is distributed across the community, rather than being concentrated in one person’s hands, whether that’s a “professional,” a guru, or the emotionally needy asshole who started the group and who can’t handle anybody leaving.

Part of the idea is that the person who’s helping you with your shit shouldn’t be in a position of power over whether or not you’re allowed to stay in the community, or do your work there, or house there, or have kids, or take medication, or be believed in conflicts.

Part of the idea is also that there are some things that peers shouldn’t be doing, and knowing what they are, and being able to direct people to outside or expert assistance when necessary.

Part of the idea is also that jealousy and conflicts get dealt with before they ever become “issues” that require parling around at the bottom of a meeting agenda.

The Romance Guide is useful for handling the dyads that will inevitably form in a community, whether or not they’re discussed in the founding document.
e19-emuA:
Things are not always so clear-cut, and there will be some crossover between the categories. But it’s useful for me to think of it this way when I’m trying to identify what my community might need to work on. So even though they’re not watertight boxes, I put the ideas in boxes to make sure I don’t miss anything.

Some stability in agreements is needed for a community to function well, but the agreements need to be flexible enough to…
e19-emuB:
There is going to be bleed through between these “categories” – i.e. how people deal with jealousy is going to be intertwined with how people run the community, how people use common things, how people parent, how people deal with medicine etc. But I do think they can be broken up like this for some degree of analysis so that people can see which “boxes” they are neglecting.

While I do agree that the agreements need to be somewhat set, I do not think that they can not be changed.
e20-emuA:
These topics aren’t as sexy or as spiritually driven. One is not likely to have an ecstatic vision about how the group needs to evolve its process for dealing with provisional members. One won’t receive a vision about how much money a departing member should be paid for their share, how land ownership should be held so that one founder doesn’t retain control, or how to proceed when a child reports something serious.

But no amount of gorgeous land will make up for the mess that is created when one person owns the land and has the final say about what will happen on it. No amount of peer counseling can make up for the mess that is created when members come on board faster than the group can support them. No amount of medicine can make up for the lack of a written exit agreement.

The first three parts will only work if they are held in a good container.

Don’t skip this part – the group will end up having to deal with it under pressure anyway.
e20-emuB:
These topics tend to get less spiritual juice put into them. It is rare that someone comes back from an ecstatic vision saying, “The spirits want a better process for bringing in provisional members!” Or, “The angels say, this is how to split up the equity of someone leaving the community!” Or, “It came to this child in a vision – this is how to deal with when a child discloses something serious.”

The beauty of the land can’t make up for having the land in one person’s name. Strong peer counseling can’t help if the membership process is not set up properly. The healing power of medicine can’t fix it if an agreement wasn’t made with someone leaving the community.

The first 3 parts are the inside of the container, and this is the container itself.

Neglect this, and it will catch up to the community eventually.
